references.text: Jeremiah prophesies about nations that must bow their necks under the yoke of the king of Babylon, which is an iron yoke of slavery.
The Lord says he has placed an iron yoke on the necks of all peoples so that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar, directly fulfilling the threats in Deuteronomy.
Isaiah describes Israel as servants to enemies, where the Lord gave his people into the hand of their foe, reflecting the punishment in Deuteronomy.
Rehoboam threatens to make the people's yoke heavier and punish them with scorpions, illustrating submission under harsh masters.
Lamentations describes the extreme hunger and thirst during Jerusalem's siege, where even infants suffer and women cook their own children.
The continuation of the curses in the same chapter, where Israel will be led back to Egypt as slaves, expands on the theme of slavery under enemies.
A parallel curse in Leviticus concerning hunger and lack of bread as punishment for disobedience.
Ezekiel prophesies that the staff of bread will be broken in Jerusalem, and the people shall eat bread by weight and drink water by measure in anguish.
